###  The purpose of this script is to
-  Make a function that helps plotting
-  Make a function that helps tidy data

###  Functions
-  phycount(data, column) |
Returns a dataframe of your column, and its group count
-  taxonplot(data, column) |
Returns a plotly widget bar graph of said group count

##  Libraries
```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytuesdayR)
library(plotly)
```

##  Data
```{r}
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load(2026, week = 41)
# ^ tidytuesday data requires you to load in both the dfs of the week
# v and read in the dataset you're interested in
frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb <- tuesdata$frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb
```

*Taking a look at the data*
```{r}
str(frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb)

glimpse(frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb)
```
Lots of NAs here, I'm going to plot counts of different taxonomic levels

##  Functions

*Building a function to easliy count and sort taxonomic observations, returning the resulting dataframe*
```{r}
#making a function that extracts a count of a certain subset of taxonomic data

#data = your original data frame, x = the taxonomic observation <chr>
phycount = function(data, taxa) { 
  df <- data |>
    select({{taxa}}) |>
    drop_na() |>
    group_by({{taxa}}) |>
    summarize(member_count = n()) |>
    arrange(desc(member_count))
    return(df)
}

```
Hooray! Lets see if it works!
```{r}
phycount(frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb, specificepithet) #Species~ish
phycount(frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb, genus) #genus
phycount(frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb, family) #family
phycount(frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb, subfamily) #subfamily, which in this case is bigger than family
phycount(frogs_and_toads_amphibiaweb, ordr) #order, which I guess they named that way because calling things "order" in your df would lead to some nightmare headaches. Definitely stealing this tip.
```
It does!!!!

phycount() will be more useful than glimpse() or head() for a quick view of taxonomic diversity at any level. For me, it'll be useful as a method to ideate which level (species, family, subfamily, order) to use for plotting!

Plus, I avoid 7 lines of code for each taxonomic level :p


*Plotting functions*
```{r}
taxonplot = function(df, taxa) {
      
  to_ggplot <- phycount(df, {{taxa}})
                #Nested function finally works!!! Hooray!!
  
  to_plotly <- ggplot(data = to_ggplot, aes(
          x = {{taxa}},
          y = member_count,
       fill = {{taxa}})) +
      geom_col() +
      theme( 
            axis.text.x = element_blank()) +
      #guides(fill = "none") +
      labs(y = "Member Count",
           )

ggplotly(to_plotly)
    
}
```
taxonplot() will quickly visualize the disparity in observations based on the taxonomic level you throw to it.

Extra useful that it reads the same variables as phycount() so if you know one you can do the other.
